tutorials.record.title: record audio
tutorials.record.driver_windows: on windows, pick asio if your interface came with an asio driver: it's the fastest. wasapi works with every device.
tutorials.record.driver_mac: on a mac there is one driver, core audio, and it works well with every interface.
tutorials.record.driver_linux: on linux, pipewire or jack give the shortest delays; alsa talks to the hardware directly.
tutorials.record.intro.title: record your voice or instrument
tutorials.record.intro.p1: we'll set up your sound device, make a track to record on, check your level and record a first take. you need a microphone (your computer's built-in one is fine) or an instrument plugged into an audio interface. headphones help a lot.
tutorials.record.intro.browser: in the browser, ethereal can't record yet: recording needs the desktop app. follow along anyway: everything here works the same way there.
tutorials.record.interface.title: what is an audio interface?
tutorials.record.interface.p1: it's the box between your instruments and your computer. it turns the sound of a microphone or a guitar into numbers the computer can record, and turns the computer's numbers back into sound for your headphones and speakers.
tutorials.record.interface.p2: your laptop's built-in microphone and speakers are a small audio interface too. a usb interface adds better sound, proper microphone inputs, inputs for guitar or bass (often marked "inst" or "hi-z"), a gain knob per input and a headphone output.
tutorials.record.io.title: inputs, outputs, mono and stereo
tutorials.record.io.in_out: inputs bring sound in (a mic, a guitar, a keyboard). outputs send it out (headphones, speakers).
tutorials.record.io.numbers: an interface numbers its inputs: input 1, input 2… with the mic in input 1 and the guitar in input 2, each one is recorded on its own track.
tutorials.record.io.mono_stereo: one mic or one guitar is mono: one input. a stereo keyboard or a pair of mics uses two inputs together, a stereo pair such as 3/4.
tutorials.record.open_settings.title: open the settings
tutorials.record.open_settings.body: your sound device is chosen in the settings, behind this gear.
tutorials.record.audio_tab.title: the audio tab
tutorials.record.audio_tab.body: everything about your sound device lives in this tab.
tutorials.record.browser_devices.title: in the browser, your system chooses
tutorials.record.browser_devices.p1: a web page can't pick sound devices: ethereal plays through the output your computer's sound settings use (and, in the desktop app, records from the input you choose here).
tutorials.record.browser_devices.p2: to use an audio interface in the browser, make it the default device in your system's sound settings.
tutorials.record.browser_devices.fallbac: a web page can't pick sound devices: ethereal plays through the output your computer's sound settings use.
tutorials.record.output.title: where the sound comes out
tutorials.record.output.body: the output device is what you listen on: your interface (plug your headphones or speakers into it) or the computer's own speakers.
tutorials.record.input.title: where the sound comes in
tutorials.record.input.p1: the input device is what you record from: your interface, or the built-in microphone. "(2 ch)" means it has two inputs. with "none", nothing can be recorded.
tutorials.record.input.p2: usually the input and the output are the same interface.
tutorials.record.sample_rate.title: sample rate: how often sound is measured
tutorials.record.sample_rate.body: your voice is recorded as tens of thousands of measurements per second. 44,100 hz (as on a compact disc) and 48,000 hz (video) both sound great. higher rates take more computer power and disk space for little you can hear. not sure? keep what's there.
tutorials.record.buffer.title: buffer size: delay or safety
tutorials.record.buffer.p1: the computer handles sound in small batches. a small buffer (64 or 128 samples) means a short delay between playing a note and hearing it, which matters when you listen to yourself while recording. it also makes the computer work harder.
tutorials.record.buffer.p2: hear clicks, pops or crackles? those are dropouts: raise the buffer (256, 512). while mixing with lots of effects a big buffer is fine. the line below shows the delay (latency) in milliseconds: under about 10 ms feels instant.
tutorials.record.input_check.title: the input check
tutorials.record.input_check.body: once a track is ready to record, its level shows here too: handy to check that the sound arrives.
tutorials.record.close_settings.title: close the settings
tutorials.record.close_settings.body: your choices are saved right away.
tutorials.record.add_track.title: make an audio track
tutorials.record.add_track.body: recordings go on an audio track (midi tracks hold notes for instruments instead). each recording becomes a clip on it.
tutorials.record.inputs.title: the recording inputs
tutorials.record.inputs.body: this button opens the list of your tracks with what each one records from.
tutorials.record.arm.title: choose the input, then arm
tutorials.record.arm.input: input: the number your mic or guitar is plugged into. one input (in 1) for mono, a pair (1/2) for stereo.
tutorials.record.arm.monitor: monitor is hearing yourself through the computer. "auto": while the track is armed. "in": always. "off": never (when your interface lets you hear yourself directly).
tutorials.record.arm.headphones: monitor with headphones: with speakers, the mic picks up its own sound and it can howl (feedback).
tutorials.record.arm.arming: arming (●) gets a track ready: it records when you press record.
tutorials.record.arm.arming_browser: arming (●) gets a track ready: it records when you press record. in the browser you can arm it, but not record.
tutorials.record.arm.fallback: open the inputs (the in button at the top), pick the input of your audio track and arm it with ●.
tutorials.record.level.title: check your level
tutorials.record.level.p1: make some sound: sing, talk, play. the meter on the right edge of the track moves. no movement? check the input number and that the interface's input is on.
tutorials.record.level.p2: set the level with the gain knob on your interface, not the track's volume (that only changes playback). play your loudest part: the peaks should reach the upper middle, never the top. too quiet means hiss when you turn it up later; too loud means clipping, a harsh distortion you can't remove afterwards.
tutorials.record.record.title: record
tutorials.record.record.body: press record. with a count-in (next to it) you get a bar or two of clicks before the recording starts. play your part!
tutorials.record.stop.title: stop when you're done
tutorials.record.stop.body: press ● again, or the space bar, to stop.
tutorials.record.take.title: your first take
tutorials.record.take.p1: the new clip on the track is your first take. play it back with the space bar or the play button.
tutorials.record.take.p2: record again over the same spot and each pass is kept: the takes button on the track shows them in lanes, so you can pick the best bits of each and build one perfect take (that's called comping). undo removes a take you don't want.
tutorials.record.browser_record.title: recording needs the desktop app
tutorials.record.browser_record.body: in the browser the record button stays grey: a web page can't record your interface yet. install the desktop app to record, and everything you saw here works the same way.
tutorials.record.done.title: that's it
tutorials.record.done.body: you know your way around recording now. the "record audio tutorial" project stays in your projects: open it any time to listen back or keep going.
tutorials.first_track.intro.title: make your first track
tutorials.first_track.intro.p1: in a few steps you'll make a track, give it an instrument, write a clip of notes and play it.
tutorials.first_track.intro.p2: you need nothing else: the instruments come with ethereal, no samples or plugins needed.
tutorials.first_track.add_track.title: add a midi track
tutorials.first_track.add_track.body: a midi track plays notes on an instrument. (an audio track holds recordings and samples instead.)
tutorials.first_track.instrument.title: pick an instrument
tutorials.first_track.instrument.p1: the track already has the synth on it. the poly synth is a richer one, with presets: basses, keys, pads, even drums.
tutorials.first_track.instrument.p2: the sampler and the drum rack play sounds you bring: keep them for later.
tutorials.first_track.instrument.fallbac: the track plays the built-in synth. you can change it any time in the inspector, on the right.
tutorials.first_track.window.title: its window
tutorials.first_track.window.body: the instrument opens in a window: its knobs shape the sound. you'll come back to it. the tour closes it to make room for the next step.
tutorials.first_track.clip.title: make a clip
tutorials.first_track.clip.body: a clip holds notes, on the track's lane. double-click the empty lane near the start: a one-bar clip appears. hold the second click and drag to make it longer.
tutorials.first_track.open_clip.title: open it
tutorials.first_track.open_clip.body: double-click the clip: it opens in the piano roll, at the bottom of the window.
tutorials.first_track.notes.title: draw some notes
tutorials.first_track.notes.add: rows are pitches (the keyboard on the left), columns are time. double-click an empty spot to add a note: you hear it.
tutorials.first_track.notes.edit: drag a note to move it, drag its right edge to make it longer, double-click it to delete it.
tutorials.first_track.play.title: play it
tutorials.first_track.play.body: playback starts where the playhead is and goes on until you stop it. the space bar plays and stops too.
tutorials.first_track.stop.title: and stop
tutorials.first_track.stop.body: the same button stops, and the playhead goes back to where it started.
tutorials.first_track.done.title: that's your first track
tutorials.first_track.done.p1: it stays in your projects as "my first track". ethereal saves as you go.
tutorials.first_track.done.p2: the guide in the documentation goes on from here: a second instrument, an effect, a loop to play over and over.
